Additionally, [`_fix_orphaned_tool_messages()`](lobster/agents/context_management.py#L245-L289) strips any `ToolMessage` at the start of the trimmed list whose corresponding `AIMessage(tool_calls)` was dropped by trimming — preventing LLM API rejections from invalid chat history.

The **agent result memory** system works in concert: when `_invoke_and_store()` dual-writes a delegation result to `InMemoryStore`, the `store_key` survives message trimming because it's registered in `OverallState.store_keys` (populated by the pre-model hook). The supervisor can later call `retrieve_agent_result(store_key=...)` to access the full data without asking the user to repeat information.

Sources: [context_management.py](lobster/agents/context_management.py#L117-L168), [context_management.py](lobster/agents/context_management.py#L245-L358), [graph.py](lobster/agents/graph.py#L815-L847)

## SupervisorConfig: Environment-Driven Behavior Modes

The [`SupervisorConfig`](lobster/config/supervisor_config.py#L18-L69) dataclass controls every aspect of supervisor behavior through environment variables following the `SUPERVISOR_<SETTING_NAME>` pattern. The configuration spans five domains:

| Domain | Key Settings | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Interaction** | `ask_clarification_questions`, `max_clarification_questions`, `require_download_confirmation`, `require_metadata_preview` | `True`, `2`, `True`, `True` |
| **Response** | `auto_suggest_next_steps`, `verbose_delegation`, `summarize_expert_output` | `True`, `True`, `False` |
| **Context** | `include_data_context`, `include_system_info`, `include_memory_stats` | `True`, `False`, `False` |
| **Workflow** | `delegation_strategy`, `workflow_guidance_level`, `enable_todo_planning` | `"auto"`, `"detailed"`, `True` |
| **Security** | `admin_mode` | `False` |

The `get_prompt_mode()` method summarizes the configuration into one of four named modes: **Production** (no questions, minimal guidance), **Development** (verbose delegation, detailed guidance), **Research** (questions enabled, detailed guidance), or **Standard** (everything else). The `interactive` flag (passed separately, not from config) controls whether `ask_user` tools are available — when `False`, the supervisor operates in single-query mode with no HITL capabilities.

Sources: [supervisor_config.py](lobster/config/supervisor_config.py#L18-L69), [supervisor_config.py](lobster/config/supervisor_config.py#L71-L132), [supervisor_config.py](lobster/config/supervisor_config.py#L204-L224)

## Graph Construction: The Complete Pipeline

The [`create_bioinformatics_graph()`](lobster/agents/graph.py#L678-L920) function orchestrates the full pipeline from configuration to compiled graph:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Auto-detect<br/>subscription tier] --> B[Create supervisor<br/>LLM via create_llm]
    B --> C[_resolve_worker_agents<br/>3-stage filtering]
    C --> D[_create_agents_single_pass<br/>eager + lazy tools]
    D --> E[_build_supervisor_tools<br/>handoff + utility]
    E --> F[create_supervisor_prompt<br/>7-section assembly]
    F --> G[Context management<br/>budget + pre_model_hook]
    G --> H[create_react_agent<br/>supervisor ReAct loop]
    H --> I[StateGraph wrapper<br/>single-node topology]
    I --> J[AQUADIF monitoring<br/>tool metadata map]
    J --> K[Return<br/>graph + GraphMetadata]

    style C fill:#7c3aed,stroke:#5b21b6,color:#fff
    style D fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,color:#fff
    style F fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,color:#fff
    style H fill:#2563eb,stroke:#1e40af,color:#fff
```

Key design decisions in this pipeline:

1. **Agent creation is single-pass**: All agents are created in one loop (`_create_agents_single_pass`), with lazy delegation tools capturing the shared `created_agents` dict by reference. Failed agents are removed from `worker_agents` before downstream phases see them.

2. **Supervisor prompt is built after agents exist**: The `active_agents` list passed to `create_supervisor_prompt()` is the `supervisor_accessible_names` list from `_build_supervisor_tools()`, ensuring the prompt only references agents that actually have handoff tools.

3. **Context management is conditional on store**: The `pre_model_hook` is only created when `InMemoryStore` is provided. Without it, no trimming or store key injection occurs — the supervisor relies on the LLM's native context handling.

4. **The graph topology is trivially simple**: A `StateGraph` with a single `"supervisor"` node. All complexity lives inside the ReAct agent's tool selection loop, not in graph edges. This makes the system easier to debug and extend — adding a new agent requires only a registry entry and a handoff tool, no graph restructuring.

Sources: [graph.py](lobster/agents/graph.py#L678-L920)

## What's Next

The supervisor agent is the routing brain, but its intelligence depends on the state it reads and the agents it discovers. To understand the full picture:

- **[LangGraph State and Graph Topology](6-langgraph-state-and-graph-topology)** — How `OverallState`, `TodoItem`, and the state reducer pattern enable the supervisor's planning and handoff mechanisms.
- **[Agent Registry and Discovery](7-agent-registry-and-discovery)** — How `ComponentRegistry` discovers agents via entry points and how `AgentRegistryConfig` defines the routing contract.
- **[Security Policy and Instruction Hierarchy](21-security-policy-and-instruction-hierarchy)** — The immutable security policy that sits above all supervisor routing decisions.

# LangGraph State and Graph Topology



Lobster's multi-agent system is built on **LangGraph's Tool Calling pattern**, where a supervisor ReAct agent orchestrates domain specialist sub-agents through dynamically generated handoff tools. This page dissects the three pillars that make the graph tick: the **state schema** that flows through every node, the **graph topology** that wires supervisor to specialists, and the **context management pipeline** that keeps the system from overflowing its token budget. Understanding these mechanisms is essential for anyone extending the agent registry, adding domain packages, or debugging handoff failures.

## State Schema Architecture

The state layer follows a deliberate **extensible base class** pattern. `OverallState` extends LangGraph's `AgentState` with routing metadata, task context, and a todo list — and every specialist agent receives a state schema that either is `OverallState` (for the supervisor) or a domain-specific subclass of `AgentState` (for workers). The critical design decision is that the supervisor and its sub-graphs share the `OverallState` schema at the top level, while individual agents carry their own richer state internally.

### OverallState: The Graph-Wide Contract

`OverallState` is the single state object that traverses the `StateGraph`. It carries everything the supervisor needs to route requests and track progress:

| Field | Type | Reducer | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `messages` | `list[BaseMessage]` | `add_messages` (inherited) | Conversation history — inherited from `AgentState` |
| `last_active_agent` | `str` | Default (replace) | Name of the agent that last handled the conversation |
| `conversation_id` | `str` | Default (replace) | Unique session identifier |
| `current_task` | `str` | Default (replace) | Current task description for cross-agent handoffs |
| `task_context` | `Dict[str, Any]` | Default (replace) | Additional context passed between agents |
| `todos` | `Annotated[List[TodoItem], _todo_reducer]` | `_todo_reducer` (replace) | Task list managed via `write_todos` tool |
| `store_keys` | `Dict[str, str]` | Default (replace) | Registry of store keys from sub-agent delegations |
| `context_compaction` | `Dict[str, Any]` | Default (replace) | Metadata emitted when `pre_model_hook` trims context |

The `todos` field uses a **replace reducer** (`_todo_reducer`) rather than an append reducer, because the todo list represents the *current plan state*, not an append-only history. The supervisor sends a complete updated list on each `write_todos` call, matching the DeepAgents/LangChain `TodoListMiddleware` behavior.

Sources: [state.py](/lobster/agents/state.py#L68-L131)

### TodoItem: Planning Primitive

Each `TodoItem` tracks a single subtask within a multi-step pipeline:

```python
class TodoItem(TypedDict):
    content: str      # "Download GSE12345"
    status: str       # "pending" | "in_progress" | "completed"
    activeForm: str   # "Downloading GSE12345" (present continuous for UI)
```

The supervisor creates these via the `write_todos` tool *before* delegating to any agent in a multi-step pipeline (cognitive protocol classification C). This gives the UI real-time progress visibility and gives the supervisor a structured way to resume after errors without restarting from step one.

Sources: [state.py](/lobster/agents/state.py#L82-L109)

### Domain-Specific State Schemas

Specialist agents carry their own state classes that extend `AgentState` with domain fields. These schemas are **not** shared with the supervisor — they exist within each agent's internal ReAct loop. The pattern is consistent across all domain states:

| State Class | Package | Key Domain Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `SingleCellExpertState` | Core (legacy) | `clustering_parameters`, `cell_type_annotations`, `marker_genes`, `doublet_detection_results` |
| `BulkRNASeqExpertState` | Core (legacy) | `differential_expression_results`, `pathway_enrichment_results`, `experimental_design` |
| `MethodState` | Core | `methods_information`, `evaluation_metrics`, `recommendations` |
| `CustomFeatureAgentState` | Core | `feature_type`, `created_files`, `sdk_output`, `validation_errors` |
| `TranscriptomicsExpertState` | `lobster-transcriptomics` | Discovered via `lobster.states` entry points |
| `ProteomicsExpertState` | `lobster-proteomics` | Discovered via `lobster.states` entry points |
| `ResearchAgentState` | `lobster-research` | Discovered via `lobster.states` entry points |

Every domain state includes a `next: str` field (for potential graph-internal routing), `task_description`, `data_context`, `file_paths`, `methodology_parameters`, and `intermediate_outputs` — providing a uniform interface for partial computation handoffs back to the supervisor.

Sources: [state.py](/lobster/agents/state.py#L133-L266)

### Dynamic State Discovery via Entry Points

Domain packages register their state classes through the `lobster.states` entry point group. The `get_all_state_classes()` function resolves the full state catalog at runtime:

```python
def get_all_state_classes() -> Dict[str, Type]:
    states: Dict[str, Type] = {}
    # Core states from this module
    # ...
    # Discover package states via entry points
    eps = entry_points(group="lobster.states")
    for ep in eps:
        state_class = ep.load()
        states[ep.name] = state_class
    return states
```

This means adding a new domain package with its own state schema requires zero changes to the core graph module — the state class is discovered and registered automatically when the package is installed.

Sources: [state.py](/lobster/agents/state.py#L20-L64)

## Graph Topology: The Tool Calling Pattern

Lobster uses LangGraph's **Tool Calling** multi-agent pattern, which is fundamentally simpler than the Handoffs pattern. The supervisor is a single ReAct agent; sub-agents are invoked as tools. There is no graph-based routing between specialist nodes — the LLM itself decides which handoff tool to call based on tool descriptions. The user only ever interacts with the supervisor.

### Topology Diagram

Before examining the diagram, understand the key architectural constraint: the `StateGraph` contains exactly **one node** (`supervisor`) between `START` and `END`. All specialist agents are *tools* of that node, not separate graph nodes. This is the Tool Calling pattern's defining characteristic — the graph topology is trivially simple, and the complexity lives in the tool layer.

```mermaid
graph TD
    START([START]) --> Supervisor
    Supervisor --> END([END])

    subgraph "Supervisor (ReAct Agent)"
        direction TB
        LLM["Supervisor LLM<br/>(create_react_agent)"]
        ToolNode["Tool Execution Layer"]
        LLM -->|"tool_call"| ToolNode
        ToolNode -->|"tool_result"| LLM
    end

    subgraph "Handoff Tools (Eager)"
        H1["handoff_to_single_cell_agent"]
        H2["handoff_to_research_agent"]
        H3["handoff_to_method_agent"]
    end

    subgraph "Handoff Tools (Lazy / Parent→Child)"
        H4["handoff_to_annotation_expert"]
        H5["handoff_to_de_analysis_expert"]
    end

    subgraph "Utility Tools"
        U1["list_available_modalities"]
        U2["execute_custom_code"]
        U3["write_todos / read_todos"]
        U4["retrieve_agent_result"]
        U5["ask_user (interactive only)"]
    end

    ToolNode --> H1 & H2 & H3
    ToolNode --> H4 & H5
    ToolNode --> U1 & U2 & U3 & U4 & U5

    H1 & H2 & H3 -->|"ainvoke + store"| SubAgents["Domain Agent<br/>(create_react_agent)"]
    H4 & H5 -->|"lazy resolve + ainvoke"| ChildAgents["Child Agent<br/>(create_react_agent)"]
```

Sources: [graph.py](/lobster/agents/graph.py#L840-L867)

### Graph Construction Pipeline

The `create_bioinformatics_graph()` function is the single entry point that assembles the entire graph. Its construction pipeline proceeds through six sequential phases:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["1. Resolve Subscription Tier"] --> B["2. Resolve Worker Agents<br/>(_resolve_worker_agents)"]
    B --> C["3. Create Agents Single Pass<br/>(_create_agents_single_pass)"]
    C --> D["4. Build Supervisor Tools<br/>(_build_supervisor_tools)"]
    D --> E["5. Context Management Setup<br/>(pre_model_hook)"]
    E --> F["6. Compile StateGraph<br/>(supervisor node → START → END)"]

    B -->|"Filter chain"| B1["enabled_agents param<br/>→ config.enabled_agents<br/>→ all discovered"]
    B1 --> B2["Auto-include child agents"]
    B2 --> B3["Tier-based agent_filter"]

    C -->|"For each agent"| C1["Import factory function"]
    C1 --> C2["Create lazy delegation tools<br/>(for child agents)"]
    C2 --> C3["Call factory with kwargs"]
    C3 --> C4["Add to created_agents dict<br/>(mutated in-place)"]
```

**Phase 1 — Tier Resolution**: If no `subscription_tier` is provided, the system auto-detects from the license manager. This tier gates which agents are available.

**Phase 2 — Worker Agent Resolution**: Applies three filters in order: (1) `enabled_agents` parameter > `config.enabled_agents` > all discovered agents, (2) auto-inclusion of child agents for enabled parents, (3) tier-based `agent_filter`. Returns `(worker_agents, filtered_out_agents, child_agent_names)`.

**Phase 3 — Single-Pass Agent Creation**: Iterates over resolved worker agents, imports each factory function, creates lazy delegation tools for parent agents with children, and calls the factory. The `created_agents` dict is **mutated in-place** — this is critical because lazy delegation tools capture the dict by reference and resolve agents at invocation time.

**Phase 4 — Supervisor Tool Assembly**: Builds the supervisor's complete tool belt: handoff tools (eager for top-level agents, lazy for children), workspace tools, code execution, todo tools, and optionally `ask_user` (interactive mode only).

**Phase 5 — Context Management**: If `store` is provided, resolves the context window and budget, creates a `pre_model_hook` with `retrieve_agent_result` tool, and wires everything together.

**Phase 6 — Graph Compilation**: Creates the `StateGraph(OverallState)`, adds the single `supervisor` node, compiles with `checkpointer` and `store`, and returns `(graph, GraphMetadata)`.

Sources: [graph.py](/lobster/agents/graph.py#L673-L921)

### Eager vs. Lazy Delegation Tools

The distinction between eager and lazy delegation tools is one of the most important architectural details in the graph:

| Aspect | Eager (`_create_agent_tool`) | Lazy (`_create_lazy_delegation_tool`) |
|---|---|---|
| **Use case** | Supervisor → top-level agent handoff | Parent → child agent handoff |
| **Agent reference | Captures compiled agent instance directly | Captures `agents_dict` by reference, resolves at call time |
| **When agent exists | Must exist at tool creation time | May not exist yet (parent created before child) |
| **Failure mode | `None` — agent is guaranteed present | Returns install instructions if agent missing |
| **Tool naming | Uses `agent_config.handoff_tool_name` | Auto-generates `handoff_to_{child_name}` |
| **Category metadata | `["DELEGATE"]` | `["DELEGATE"]` |

The lazy resolution pattern exists because agents are created in a single pass without guaranteed ordering — a parent agent's factory may run before its children are compiled. The `created_agents` dict is shared by reference, so when a child delegation tool is eventually invoked, it finds the agent already populated.

> [!TIP]
> When adding a new agent with children, ensure the child agent names appear in `agent_config.child_agents` in the registry. The graph constructor auto-includes children for enabled parents and creates lazy delegation tools — but only for children listed in that config field. Missing entries mean invisible children.

Sources: [graph.py](/lobster/agents/graph.py#L202-L297)

### The Shared Invoke Pipeline

Both eager and lazy tools funnel through `_invoke_and_store()`, which provides a uniform execution pipeline:

1. **Config attribution**: Sets `run_name`, `tags`, and `metadata` on the `RunnableConfig` so nested LangGraph runs propagate the agent name for observability.
2. **Agent invocation**: Calls `agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": task_description}]}, config=config)`.
3. **Result extraction**: Pulls the final message from the response.
4. **Dual-write to store**: If `store` is provided, calls `store_delegation_result()` to persist the full response and appends `[store_key=...]` to the returned content.

The dual-write pattern is what makes `retrieve_agent_result` possible — the supervisor can recall full analysis outputs long after the conversation history has been trimmed.

Sources: [graph.py](/lobster/agents/graph.py#L161-L180)

## Context Management Pipeline

Without context management, a long multi-agent conversation would inevitably exceed the LLM's context window — tool schemas consume tokens on every call, agent responses are verbose, and the conversation grows monotonically. The `pre_model_hook` mechanism solves this with a non-destructive trimming pipeline that runs on every ReAct iteration.

### Budget Resolution

The context budget is calculated from three inputs:

```
budget = (context_window × 0.80) − tool_schema_tokens − system_prompt_tokens
```

The 20% reserve accounts for model output tokens and safety margin against counting drift. Tool schema tokens are measured explicitly (not estimated) using `measure_tool_schema_tokens()`, which serializes each tool's name, description, and JSON schema. When fixed overhead exceeds 50% of the context window, a warning is logged — this indicates the model will struggle with complex conversations.

| Parameter | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` | 128,000 tokens | Fallback when provider info unavailable |
| `OUTPUT_RESERVE_FRACTION` | 0.20 | Fraction reserved for model output |
| `MINIMUM_BUDGET` | 4,096 tokens | Absolute floor — prevents degenerate trimming |
| `BASELINE_WARNING_THRESHOLD` | 0.50 | Overhead fraction that triggers a warning |

Context window resolution follows a priority chain: workspace model override → global model override → provider catalog. This ensures that per-workspace configurations (e.g., a local Ollama model with a smaller window) take precedence over defaults.

Sources: [context_management.py](/lobster/agents/context_management.py#L17-L139)

### The pre_model_hook Execution Flow

On every ReAct iteration, the supervisor's `pre_model_hook` executes the following pipeline:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Read InMemoryStore<br/>→ build store_keys index"] --> B["Wrap tool results<br/>in <tool_data> markers"]
    B --> C["Compute effective budget<br/>(budget − key_index_overhead)"]
    C --> D["trim_messages()<br/>strategy='last', include_system=True"]
    D --> E["Fix orphaned ToolMessages"]
    E --> F{"Trimmed messages<br/>< original?"}
    F -->|Yes| G["Emit context_compaction<br/>metadata"]
    F -->|No| H["No compaction needed"]
    G --> I["Append store key index<br/>to SystemMessage"]
    H --> I
    I --> J["Return llm_input_messages<br/>+ store_keys + context_compaction"]
```

**Step 1 — Store Key Index**: Reads all stored agent results from `InMemoryStore` and builds a `key → agent_name` index. This index survives message trimming because it's injected into the `SystemMessage` rather than the conversation history.

**Step 2 — Tool Result Spotlighting**: Wraps every `ToolMessage`'s content in `<tool_data>...</tool_data>` markers. This is a **security defense** — it ensures the LLM treats tool output as inert data, not instructions. Handles both string content and multi-part list content.

**Step 3 — Budget Adjustment**: Subtracts the token cost of the key index text from the effective budget before trimming. This prevents the injected index from pushing the trimmed messages over budget.

**Step 4 — Trimming**: Uses `trim_messages()` with `strategy="last"` (trims from the front), `include_system=True` (preserves the SystemMessage), and `allow_partial=False` (no truncated messages). The custom `_message_list_token_counter` counts all token-bearing fields including `tool_calls`, `tool_call_id`, and message names.

**Step 5 — Orphan Fix**: When `trim_messages` drops an `AIMessage(tool_calls=...)` but keeps the subsequent `ToolMessage`, the result is an invalid chat history that causes LLM API rejections. `_fix_orphaned_tool_messages()` strips leading `ToolMessage` entries whose `tool_call_id` has no matching `AIMessage`.

**Step 6 — Compaction Metadata**: If any messages were trimmed, emits `context_compaction` with `before_count`, `after_count`, and `budget_tokens` — used by streaming UIs to surface compaction visibility.

> [!TIP]
> The `pre_model_hook` returns `llm_input_messages` (not `messages`), which is the non-destructive bypass in LangGraph. The original `state["messages"]` is never modified — trimmed messages are only what the LLM sees. This means the full conversation history is always recoverable from the checkpointer, even after aggressive trimming.

Sources: [context_management.py](/lobster/agents/context_management.py#L399-L473)

## GraphMetadata: API Surface

The `create_bioinformatics_graph()` function returns a `(graph, GraphMetadata)` tuple. `GraphMetadata` captures the graph's construction-time state for frontend consumption:

```python
@dataclass
class GraphMetadata:
    subscription_tier: str
    available_agents: List[AgentInfo]
    supervisor_accessible_agents: List[str]
    filtered_out_agents: List[str]
```

Each `AgentInfo` includes the agent's `name`, `display_name`, `description`, `is_supervisor_accessible`, `parent_agent`, `child_agents`, and `handoff_tool_name`. This dataclass is serializable via `to_dict()` and provides the single source of truth for what agents exist, what hierarchy they form, and what the subscription tier permits.

Sources: [graph.py](/lobster/agents/graph.py#L40-L97)

## Key Design Decisions

| Decision | Rationale | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Tool Calling over Handoffs pattern | Simpler graph topology; LLM decides routing via tool selection; user only interacts with supervisor | Less explicit control over routing; depends on LLM's tool-selection accuracy |
| Replace reducer for `todos` | Represents current plan state, not history; matches TodoListMiddleware convention | Cannot reconstruct plan history from state alone |
| Lazy delegation tools for children | Parent agents created before children; dict-by-reference allows resolution at invocation | Slight runtime overhead on first child invocation; failure path returns install instructions |
| `llm_input_messages` bypass | Non-destructive trimming preserves full history in checkpointer | Requires understanding that `state["messages"]` ≠ what the LLM sees |
| Store dual-write with key index | Full results survive trimming; LLM always knows what's available for retrieval | Additional store reads on every iteration; token overhead for key index injection |
| `<tool_data>` spotlighting | Defense against prompt injection via tool output | Slight token overhead per ToolMessage |

Sources: [graph.py](/lobster/agents/graph.py#L1-L15), [state.py](/lobster/agents/state.py#L95-L109), [context_management.py](/lobster/agents/context_management.py#L290-L340)

## What Comes Next

With the state schema and graph topology understood, the natural next step is to examine how agents are discovered, registered, and made available to the graph constructor: see [Agent Registry and Discovery](7-agent-registry-and-discovery). For the supervisor's routing logic and cognitive protocol (which drives tool selection within this topology), see [Supervisor Agent and Routing](5-supervisor-agent-and-routing). For how tools are classified and monitored within the AQUADIF framework, see [AQUADIF Tool Taxonomy](9-aquadif-tool-taxonomy).

# Agent Registry and Discovery



The Lobster platform routes every user request through a hierarchy of specialist agents—a transcriptomics expert for single-cell analysis, a research agent for literature searches, a drug discovery expert for cheminformatics, and so on. But before the supervisor can delegate, it must **discover** which agents exist, **validate** their configuration, and **assemble** them into a routable graph. The Agent Registry and Discovery subsystem is the machinery that makes this possible: it uses Python entry points to dynamically discover agents from any installed package, validate their contracts, resolve parent-child hierarchies, enforce subscription-tier gating, and surface the resulting topology to the supervisor's prompt and the LangGraph runtime. Understanding this subsystem is essential for anyone adding a new agent package, debugging why an agent doesn't appear, or reasoning about handoff validity in a multi-step workflow.

Sources: [component_registry.py](/lobster/core/component_registry.py#L1-L79), [agent_registry.py](/lobster/config/agent_registry.py#L1-L40)

## Discovery Architecture: Entry Points as the Single Source of Truth

Lobster eliminated a once-hardcoded agent dictionary in favor of **dynamic entry-point discovery**. Every agent—whether it ships in the core `lobster-ai` package or in a separate PyPI package like `lobster-transcriptomics`—advertises itself through a `[project.entry-points."lobster.agents"]` declaration in its `pyproject.toml`. At runtime, the `ComponentRegistry` singleton scans this entry-point group, loads each `AGENT_CONFIG` object, and indexes it by name. This means installing a new agent package is sufficient for it to appear in the system; no central registry file needs editing.

The entry-point groups that `ComponentRegistry` scans are codified in a single tuple, and each group maps to a dedicated internal dictionary. The `lobster.agents` group is the one relevant here—it stores fully-loaded `AgentRegistryConfig` instances:

| Entry-Point Group | Stored Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `lobster.agents` | `AgentRegistryConfig` | Agent configuration and routing metadata |
| `lobster.services` | Service class | Premium feature services |
| `lobster.adapters` | Factory callable | Data modality adapters |
| `lobster.providers` | Class/callable | External data providers |
| `lobster.download_services` | Class/callable | Dataset download services |
| `lobster.queue_preparers` | Class/callable | Download queue preparation |

Loading is **idempotent and lazy**—`_ensure_group_loaded` checks whether a group has already been scanned before re-scanning, and the `load_components` method returns immediately once all groups are populated. This design ensures that even if `component_registry.list_agents()` is called from multiple initialization paths, discovery runs exactly once per group.

Sources: [component_registry.py](/lobster/core/component_registry.py#L94-L132), [component_registry.py](/lobster/core/component_registry.py#L288-L330)

## AgentRegistryConfig: The Agent's Identity Card

Every discovered agent is represented as an `AgentRegistryConfig` dataclass—a structured declaration of who the agent is, how to reach it, and what constraints govern its use. The fields divide naturally into identity, routing, hierarchy, and contract categories:

```
AgentRegistryConfig
├── Identity
│   ├── name                  # Unique identifier (e.g., "transcriptomics_expert")
│   ├── display_name          # UI label (e.g., "Transcriptomics Expert")
│   └── description           # Capability summary for the supervisor
├── Routing
│   ├── factory_function      # Module path to the agent's factory (e.g., "lobster.agents.x:create_x")
│   ├── handoff_tool_name     # Tool name for delegation (e.g., "handoff_to_transcriptomics_expert")
│   └── handoff_tool_description  # When-to-use description for the supervisor's tool selection
├── Hierarchy
│   ├── child_agents          # Agents this one can delegate to (e.g., ["annotation_expert"])
│   └── supervisor_accessible # None=infer, True/False=explicit override
└── Contract (AQUADIF Phase 2)
    ├── tier_requirement      # "free", "premium", or "enterprise"
    ├── package_name          # Owning PyPI package (e.g., "lobster-transcriptomics")
    └── service_dependencies  # Required runtime services
```

The **`supervisor_accessible`** field is particularly nuanced. When left as `None` (the default), the system *infers* accessibility: if the agent's name appears in *any* other agent's `child_agents` list, it is treated as a child-only agent and hidden from the supervisor's direct routing. Setting it to `True` overrides this inference (useful for agents that are both supervisor-accessible and children of another agent), while `False` explicitly hides the agent from the supervisor regardless of hierarchy.

Sources: [agent_registry.py](/lobster/config/agent_registry.py#L26-L65)

## The Discovery Pipeline: From Entry Point to Routable Agent

The full lifecycle from "package installed" to "supervisor can delegate" follows a precise pipeline. Understanding each stage is critical for debugging missing agents or contract violations:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Package installed<br/>with lobster.agents<br/>entry point"] --> B["ComponentRegistry<br/>scans entry points"]
    B --> C{"Version<br/>compatibility<br/>check"}
    C -->|Incompatible| D["Skip with warning<br/>(external packages only)"]
    C -->|Compatible| E["Load AGENT_CONFIG<br/>from entry point"]
    E --> F["_annotate_agent_package()<br/>Populate package_name<br/>if missing"]
    F --> G{"Name collision<br/>check"}
    G -->|Custom shadows first-party| H["ComponentConflictError<br/>raised"]
    G -->|No collision| I["Agent stored in<br/>_agents dict"]
    I --> J["Contract compliance<br/>soft check<br/>(warn on missing fields)"]
    J --> K["Agent available via<br/>list_agents(), get_agent()"]
```

**Version compatibility** is checked only for external packages (not `lobster-ai` itself). The `check_plugin_compatibility` function inspects the package's declared dependency on `lobster-ai` and verifies the installed version satisfies any `>=` constraint. Incompatible plugins are silently skipped with a warning—this prevents runtime crashes from stale packages while allowing the rest of the system to function.

**Name collision detection** rejects custom packages that shadow first-party agent names. If a package named `lobster-custom-x` tries to register an agent called `transcriptomics_expert`—a name reserved for the `lobster-transcriptomics` package—the registry raises a `ComponentConflictError`. This protects the integrity of the agent namespace.

**Contract compliance checking** is intentionally soft: agents missing `tier_requirement` or other AQUADIF fields receive a warning but are not blocked. This preserves backward compatibility with pre-AQUADIF agents while encouraging migration.

Sources: [component_registry.py](/lobster/core/component_registry.py#L330-L430), [component_registry.py](/lobster/core/component_registry.py#L430-L470)

## The Facade Layer: Backward Compatibility Without Compromise

The `agent_registry.py` module serves as a **backward-compatible facade** over `ComponentRegistry`. All of its public functions—`get_all_agent_names()`, `get_worker_agents()`, `get_agent_registry_config()`—delegate internally to `component_registry.list_agents()` or `component_registry.get_agent()`. This design decision means that any code written against the old `AGENT_REGISTRY` dict continues to work, while all discovery logic flows through the single source of truth.

The facade also provides **handoff validation** through `get_valid_handoffs()` and `is_valid_handoff()`. These functions construct a directed adjacency map by examining every agent's `child_agents` list and the `supervisor_accessible` inference logic:

| Agent | Valid Handoff Targets |
|---|---|
| `supervisor` | All supervisor-accessible agents (inferred or explicit) |
| `transcriptomics_expert` | `annotation_expert`, `de_analysis_expert` |
| `research_agent` | `metadata_assistant` |
| `data_expert_agent` | `metadata_assistant` |
| Agents with no `child_agents` | ∅ (empty set) |

The `_AgentRegistryProxy` class provides dict-like access (`__getitem__`, `__contains__`, `keys()`, `values()`, `items()`) for legacy code that imports `AGENT_REGISTRY` directly. Each access lazily delegates to `ComponentRegistry`, so the proxy is never stale.

Sources: [agent_registry.py](/lobster/config/agent_registry.py#L73-L170)

## Agent Hierarchy and the Supervisor's Agent Directory

Agents are not a flat list—they form a **tree structure** that the supervisor renders into its prompt as the *Agent Directory*. The `_build_agent_directory` function in `supervisor.py` constructs this tree by separating top-level (supervisor-accessible) agents from their children, then rendering each parent with indented sub-agents:

```
├── Transcriptomics Expert (transcriptomics_expert)
│   Expert in single-cell and bulk RNA-seq analysis...
│   Keywords: scRNA-seq, clustering, DE analysis
│   ├── Annotation Expert (annotation_expert)
│   └── DE Analysis Expert (de_analysis_expert)
├── Research Agent (research_agent)
│   Literature search and knowledge retrieval...
```

This tree is built dynamically from the **currently active** agent set—not the full registry. The `active_agents` list passed to `create_supervisor_prompt` is resolved at graph construction time by `_resolve_worker_agents`, which applies three sequential filters:

1. **Enabled-agent filter**: The `enabled_agents` parameter overrides `WorkspaceAgentConfig.enabled_agents`, which in turn falls back to "all discovered agents" when neither is specified.
2. **Auto-include children**: When a parent agent is enabled, its `child_agents` are automatically pulled in—even if they weren't explicitly listed. This prevents broken handoff chains.
3. **Tier-based gating**: Each agent's `tier_requirement` is checked against the user's subscription tier. Agents above the current tier are filtered out and recorded in `GraphMetadata.filtered_out_agents`.

> [!TIP]
> When a parent agent is enabled but its child agent's package isn't installed, the directory renders the child as "(not installed)" rather than silently dropping it. This gives the supervisor visibility into the intended hierarchy and allows it to suggest installation when a user requests a capability that requires the missing child.

Sources: [supervisor.py](/lobster/agents/supervisor.py#L115-L185), [graph.py](/lobster/agents/graph.py#L268-L335)

## Graph Construction: From Registry to Routable Topology

The `graph.py` module bridges the registry and the LangGraph runtime. Its `build_graph` function (or its async equivalent) orchestrates the full assembly:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["ComponentRegistry<br/>list_agents()"] --> B["_resolve_worker_agents()<br/>Filter + tier gate"]
    B --> C["_create_agents_single_pass()<br/>Instantiate each agent"]
    C --> D["Create handoff tools<br/>_create_agent_tool()<br/>_create_lazy_delegation_tool()"]
    D --> E["Create supervisor<br/>with all handoff tools"]
    E --> F["Compile StateGraph<br/>with checkpointer + store"]
    F --> G["Return graph +<br/>GraphMetadata"]
```

Each agent in the filtered `worker_agents` dict is instantiated via its `factory_function`, which is dynamically imported using `import_agent_factory`. The resulting compiled agent is then wrapped in one of two tool types:

- **`_create_agent_tool`**: For supervisor → agent handoffs. The agent is already created, so invocation is immediate.
- **`_create_lazy_delegation_tool`**: For parent → child handoffs. The child agent may not exist at tool-creation time (e.g., the parent was created first), so resolution is deferred to invocation time. If the child isn't found, the tool returns a diagnostic message including the install command for the missing package.

> [!TIP]
> The lazy delegation tool captures the shared `agents_dict` **by reference**, not by value. This means when the child agent is later created and added to the dict, the tool automatically resolves it on next invocation—no re-registration needed. This pattern is what allows single-pass agent creation without topological sorting.

The `GraphMetadata` dataclass captures the state of the graph at creation time for API exposure. It records the subscription tier, all available `AgentInfo` objects (with parent/child relationships), which agents the supervisor can directly access, and which were filtered out. Frontends consume this via `GraphMetadata.to_dict()` to render agent lists and capability indicators.

Sources: [graph.py](/lobster/agents/graph.py#L46-L100), [graph.py](/lobster/agents/graph.py#L130-L200), [graph.py](/lobster/agents/graph.py#L268-L335)

## Diagnostics: When an Agent Doesn't Appear

The registry provides a three-tier diagnostic model through `diagnose_missing_agent`, which distinguishes:

| Scenario | Symptom | Diagnostic Output |
|---|---|---|
| **Known agent, uninstalled package** | Entry point doesn't exist | `"Agent 'X' requires package 'Y'. Install with: uv pip install 'Y'"` |
| **Installed but broken** | Entry point exists but `load()` raises | `"Agent 'X' is installed but failed to load: <error>"` |
| **Truly unknown** | Not in `AGENT_TO_PACKAGE` mapping | `"Agent 'X' is not available. See available agents with: lobster agents list"` |

The `AGENT_TO_PACKAGE` dictionary in `component_registry.py` is the static mapping that makes the first case possible. Since entry points for uninstalled packages simply don't exist, there's no dynamic way to discover which package provides a missing agent—this mapping is the only source of that information. It must be manually updated when new first-party packages are added.

The registry also tracks **failed entry points** in `_failed_entries`, keyed by `(group, name)` tuples. This allows post-hoc inspection: `component_registry.get_failed_entry_points()` returns all agents that were discovered but couldn't be loaded, along with their error messages. The `get_info()` method provides a comprehensive diagnostic snapshot including counts, names, and failure details for all component types.

Sources: [component_registry.py](/lobster/core/component_registry.py#L180-L240), [component_registry.py](/lobster/core/component_registry.py#L680-L740)

## The Package-to-Agent Map

The `AGENT_TO_PACKAGE` dictionary serves as the authoritative mapping from agent entry-point names to their owning PyPI packages. This is essential context for understanding which packages provide which capabilities:

| Package | Agents |
|---|---|
| `lobster-research` | `research_agent`, `data_expert_agent` |
| `lobster-transcriptomics` | `transcriptomics_expert`, `annotation_expert`, `de_analysis_expert` |
| `lobster-visualization` | `visualization_expert_agent` |
| `lobster-metadata` | `metadata_assistant` |
| `lobster-structural-viz` | `protein_structure_visualization_expert` |
| `lobster-genomics` | `genomics_expert`, `variant_analysis_expert` |
| `lobster-proteomics` | `proteomics_expert`, `proteomics_de_analysis_expert`, `biomarker_discovery_expert` |
| `lobster-metabolomics` | `metabolomics_expert` |
| `lobster-ml` | `machine_learning_expert`, `feature_selection_expert`, `survival_analysis_expert` |
| `lobster-drug-discovery` | `drug_discovery_expert`, `cheminformatics_expert`, `clinical_dev_expert`, `pharmacogenomics_expert` |

Each of these packages declares its agents under `[project.entry-points."lobster.agents"]` in its `pyproject.toml`, pointing to an `AGENT_CONFIG` variable in the package's module. The `ComponentRegistry` discovers these at load time, so the mapping above is descriptive (for human reference and diagnostics) rather than prescriptive (the actual discovery mechanism is the entry points themselves).

Sources: [component_registry.py](/lobster/core/component_registry.py#L94-L160)

## How It All Connects

The relationship between the three core modules—`ComponentRegistry`, `agent_registry.py`, and the supervisor's graph-building pipeline—follows a clean dependency chain:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph "Discovery Layer"
        CR["ComponentRegistry<br/>(singleton)"]
        CR -->|discovers via| EP["lobster.agents<br/>entry points"]
        CR -->|stores| AC["AgentRegistryConfig<br/>instances"]
    end
    subgraph "Facade Layer"
        AR["agent_registry.py"]
        AR -->|delegates to| CR
        AR -->|validates| VH["get_valid_handoffs()<br/>is_valid_handoff()"]
    end
    subgraph "Runtime Layer"
        G["graph.py"]
        G -->|resolves agents| AR
        G -->|filters by tier| RW["_resolve_worker_agents()"]
        RW -->|creates| AG["Agent instances<br/>+ handoff tools"]
        G -->|returns| GM["GraphMetadata"]
    end
    subgraph "Prompt Layer"
        S["supervisor.py"]
        S -->|builds directory| AR
        S -->|renders tree| AD["Agent Directory<br/>in supervisor prompt"]
    end
```

The `ComponentRegistry` is the foundation; the facade makes it accessible with backward-compatible APIs; the graph pipeline consumes it to build the runtime; and the supervisor prompt renderer transforms the registry into a text-based directory that the LLM actually reads. No agent exists in the system unless it flows through this entire chain.

Sources: [component_registry.py](/lobster/core/component_registry.py#L1-L79), [agent_registry.py](/lobster/config/agent_registry.py#L73-L170), [graph.py](/lobster/agents/graph.py#L268-L335), [supervisor.py](/lobster/agents/supervisor.py#L115-L185)

---

**Next steps**: Now that you understand how agents are discovered and registered, explore how the supervisor uses this registry to route requests in [Supervisor Agent and Routing](5-supervisor-agent-and-routing), or learn how the LangGraph state model carries registry metadata through the graph in [LangGraph State and Graph Topology](6-langgraph-state-and-graph-topology). If you're building a new agent package, the registration contract is detailed in [Plugin System and Entry Points](8-plugin-system-and-entry-points).

# Plugin System and Entry Points



Lobster's plugin system transforms the platform from a monolithic application into a composable ecosystem of discoverable components. At its foundation lies Python's `importlib.metadata` entry point mechanism — a standards-based discovery layer that allows domain packages (transcriptomics, genomics, proteomics, and beyond) to register agents, services, adapters, and data providers without modifying core code. The **ComponentRegistry** serves as the single orchestrator for this discovery, while the scaffold toolkit and validation suite ensure that every plugin conforms to the structural and behavioral contracts the system demands.

## Architectural Overview

The plugin architecture follows a **register-at-build-time, discover-at-runtime** pattern. Package authors declare their components via `[project.entry-points]` in `pyproject.toml`; at startup, `ComponentRegistry` scans these declarations and loads them into typed dictionaries. This separation means adding a new domain agent never requires a pull request to the core repository — it only requires publishing a package that advertises the right entry point group.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Build-Time Declaration"
        P1["lobster-transcriptomics<br/>pyproject.toml"]
        P2["lobster-genomics<br/>pyproject.toml"]
        P3["lobster-custom-*<br/>pyproject.toml"]
    end

    subgraph "Entry Point Groups"
        EP1["lobster.agents"]
        EP2["lobster.services"]
        EP3["lobster.adapters"]
        EP4["lobster.providers"]
        EP5["lobster.download_services"]
        EP6["lobster.queue_preparers"]
    end

    subgraph "Runtime Discovery"
        CR["ComponentRegistry<br/>(Singleton)"]
    end

    subgraph "Consumers"
        G["Supervisor Graph"]
        DM["DataManager"]
        DQ["Download Queue"]
    end

    P1 --> EP1
    P1 --> EP2
    P2 --> EP1
    P3 --> EP1
    P3 --> EP3
    EP1 --> CR
    EP2 --> CR
    EP3 --> CR
    EP4 --> CR
    EP5 --> CR
    EP6 --> CR
    CR -->|"get_agent()"| G
    CR -->|"get_service()"| DM
    CR -->|"get_download_service()"| DQ
```

The six entry point groups form the backbone of the system. Each group maps to a specific component type with its own loading semantics and storage dictionary inside `ComponentRegistry`.

Sources: [component_registry.py](lobster/core/component_registry.py#L1-L72), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L266-L316)

## Entry Point Groups and Their Contracts

Every entry point group enforces a distinct contract — the shape of the object that gets loaded determines how the registry stores and serves it. Understanding these contracts is essential for anyone building a plugin package.

| Group | Purpose | Entry Point Value | Loaded Object Type | Key API Method |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `lobster.agents` | Agent discovery | `module:AGENT_CONFIG` | `AgentRegistryConfig` instance | `get_agent(name)` |
| `lobster.services` | Service classes | `module:ServiceClass` | Class (instantiated by consumer) | `get_service(name)` |
| `lobster.adapters` | Data adapters | `module:factory_callable` | Factory callable → adapter instance | `get_adapter(name)` |
| `lobster.providers` | Data providers | `module:ProviderClass` | Class or factory → provider instance | `get_provider(name)` |
| `lobster.download_services` | Download backends | `module:DownloadServiceClass` | Class or factory | `get_download_service(name)` |
| `lobster.queue_preparers` | Queue preparation | `module:QueuePreparerClass` | Class or factory | `get_queue_preparer(name)` |

A critical design distinction exists between **agents** and **adapters/services**: agent entry points load an `AGENT_CONFIG` dataclass instance (a declarative configuration), while adapters, providers, and download services load classes or factory callables that the consumer instantiates. This split means agent discovery is lightweight — the registry only needs the `AgentRegistryConfig`, not the full agent graph — which keeps entry point scanning under 50ms even with many packages installed.

Sources: [component_registry.py](lobster/core/component_registry.py#L275-L345), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L266-L301)

## The ComponentRegistry: Discovery and Loading

`ComponentRegistry` is a singleton (`component_registry = ComponentRegistry()`) that provides lazy, idempotent loading for each entry point group. Calling `load_components()` iterates over all six groups; each group is loaded on first access via `_ensure_group_loaded()`, meaning unused groups (e.g., `lobster.adapters` when no adapter packages are installed) incur zero cost.

The loading sequence for each group follows a consistent pipeline:

1. **Scan** — `importlib.metadata.entry_points(group=group)` retrieves all registered entry points for that group.
2. **Compatibility check** — For external packages (not `lobster-ai` itself), `check_plugin_compatibility()` validates that the plugin's declared `lobster-ai` version constraint is satisfied. Incompatible plugins are skipped with a warning.
3. **Load** — `entry.load()` imports the target module and retrieves the object. Failed loads are captured in `_failed_entries` rather than crashing the registry.
4. **Annotate** — For agents, `_annotate_agent_package()` injects the owning package name from entry point distribution metadata, ensuring `config.package_name` is always populated even if the package author omitted it.
5. **Conflict detection** — After loading `lobster.agents`, `_check_agent_name_collisions()` rejects custom agents that shadow first-party agent names by raising `ComponentConflictError`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["entry_points(group)"] --> B{"External<br/>package?"}
    B -->|Yes| C["check_plugin_compatibility()"]
    C -->|Incompatible| D["Skip + warn"]
    C -->|Compatible| E["entry.load()"]
    B -->|No| E
    E -->|Success| F["Store in dict"]
    E -->|Failure| G["_failed_entries"]
    F --> H{"Agent<br/>group?"}
    H -->|Yes| I["_annotate_agent_package()"]
    I --> J["_check_agent_name_collisions()"]
    H -->|No| K["Done"]
    J --> K
```

> [!TIP]
> When consuming the registry, prefer `required=True` on getters like `get_agent(name, required=True)` — this produces actionable error messages that include the correct `pip install` command via `diagnose_missing_agent()`, rather than a cryptic `None` return.

Sources: [component_registry.py](lobster/core/component_registry.py#L275-L438), [component_registry.py](lobster/core/component_registry.py#L598-L777)

## AgentRegistryConfig: The Agent Declaration Contract

Every agent plugin must expose an `AGENT_CONFIG` variable at the entry point target — a dataclass instance of `AgentRegistryConfig`. This object is the agent's identity card: it tells the supervisor graph how to route tasks, what tools to provide, and what tier the agent requires.

The scaffold template demonstrates the canonical declaration pattern, with `AGENT_CONFIG` positioned **before heavy imports** (LangGraph, LangChain) to ensure that entry point discovery only loads the config, not the entire agent dependency tree:

```python
from lobster.config.agent_registry import AgentRegistryConfig

AGENT_CONFIG = AgentRegistryConfig(
    name="epigenomics_expert",
    display_name="Epigenomics Expert",
    description="Epigenomics analysis tasks",
    factory_function="lobster.agents.epigenomics.epigenomics_expert.epigenomics_expert",
    handoff_tool_name="handoff_to_epigenomics_expert",
    handoff_tool_description="Assign epigenomics tasks: epigenomics analysis",
    child_agents=None,
    supervisor_accessible=True,
    tier_requirement="free",
    package_name="lobster-epigenomics",
)

# === Heavy imports below (after AGENT_CONFIG for <50ms entry point discovery) ===
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent
```

The contract tests in `tests/test_plugin_contract.py` enforce three mandatory fields:

| Field | Purpose | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `tier_requirement` | Subscription tier gate (`"free"`, `"premium"`, `"enterprise"`) | `"free"` |
| `package_name` | Owning PyPI package for install suggestions | `None` (core) |
| `service_dependencies` | Services the agent requires at runtime | `None` |

Sources: [agent.py.j2](lobster/scaffold/templates/agent.py.j2#L1-L25), [test_plugin_contract.py](tests/test_plugin_contract.py#L93-L151)

## The Plugin Package Lifecycle: Scaffold, Validate, Publish

Lobster provides a complete toolchain for creating new plugin packages: **scaffold** generates the skeleton, **validators** enforce structural compliance, and the entry point system handles runtime discovery.

### Scaffold Generation

The `scaffold_agent()` function in `lobster/scaffold/generators/agent.py` generates a complete, buildable package from a Jinja2 template context. Given an agent name like `epigenomics_expert`, it produces:

```
lobster-epigenomics/
├── pyproject.toml          # Entry points + dependencies
├── README.md
├── lobster/
│   └── agents/
│       └── epigenomics/
│           ├── __init__.py
│           ├── epigenomics_expert.py   # AGENT_CONFIG + factory
│           ├── shared_tools.py         # @tool functions
│           ├── state.py                # State schema
│           ├── config.py
│           └── prompts.py
└── tests/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── test_contract.py
    └── conftest.py
```

> [!TIP]
> PEP 420 compliance is mandatory: no `__init__.py` may exist at the `lobster/` or `lobster/agents/` namespace boundaries. The scaffold generator enforces this automatically — the only `__init__.py` is at the domain level (`lobster/agents/epigenomics/`). Violating this breaks namespace package resolution for all installed plugins.

### Eight-Point Validation

The `validate_plugin()` function in `lobster/scaffold/validators.py` runs eight structural checks ordered by severity. Each check produces a `ValidationResult` with a pass/fail status and diagnostic message:

| # | Check | What It Catches |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | PEP 420 compliance | `__init__.py` at namespace boundaries breaks multi-package resolution |
| 2 | Entry points format | Missing `lobster.agents` group or non-`:AGENT_CONFIG` targets |
| 3 | AGENT_CONFIG position | Config after heavy imports → slow entry point scanning |
| 4 | Factory signature | Missing `data_manager`, `callback_handler`, `delegation_tools` params |
| 5 | AQUADIF metadata | `@tool` functions without `.metadata` assignments |
| 6 | Provenance calls | `provenance: True` without corresponding `log_tool_usage(ir=ir)` |
| 7 | Import boundaries | Plugin importing from `lobster.agents.*` core agents (coupling violation) |
| 8 | No ImportError guards | `try/except ImportError` in domain `__init__.py` hides dependency issues |

Checks 3 and 5–6 use AST analysis to verify code structure without importing the module, making validation safe to run on partially-implemented packages.

Sources: [agent.py](lobster/scaffold/generators/agent.py#L37-L135), [validators.py](lobster/scaffold/validators.py#L1-L62), [validators.py](lobster/scaffold/validators.py#L77-L228)

## Protocols: Structural Typing for Services and State

The plugin system uses Python `Protocol` classes (PEP 544) with `@runtime_checkable` to define contracts without requiring inheritance. This means a service or state class satisfies the protocol simply by having the right methods and attributes — no base class needed.

**`ServiceProtocol`** defines the 3-tuple return contract that all analysis services follow: `(result, stats, ir)`. The `result` is the primary output (AnnData, DataFrame), `stats` is a human-readable dictionary for logging, and `ir` is an `AnalysisStep` for provenance tracking.

**`StateProtocol`** defines the minimum contract for agent state schemas: `messages`, `last_active_agent`, and `conversation_id`. Every domain-specific state (e.g., `TranscriptomicsExpertState`) extends this implicitly by including these three fields.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class ServiceProtocol {
        <<Protocol>>
        __call__(*args, **kwargs) Tuple~T, Dict, AnalysisStep~
    }
    class StateProtocol {
        <<Protocol>>
        messages: list
        last_active_agent: str
        conversation_id: str
    }
    class ClusteringService {
        cluster(adata, resolution) Tuple
    }
    class TranscriptomicsExpertState {
        messages: list
        last_active_agent: str
        conversation_id: str
        +domain fields...
    }
    ServiceProtocol <|.. ClusteringService : satisfies
    StateProtocol <|.. TranscriptomicsExpertState : satisfies
```

Sources: [protocols.py](lobster/core/protocols.py#L1-L74)

## Version Compatibility and Conflict Resolution

The registry includes two safety mechanisms that prevent broken plugin combinations from destabilizing the system at runtime.

**Version compatibility** is checked during `_load_entry_point_group()`. For each entry point from an external package, `check_plugin_compatibility()` parses the package's dependency on `lobster-ai` and validates the `>=` version constraint against the currently installed version. Incompatible plugins are silently skipped with a warning — the system degrades gracefully rather than crashing.

**Name collision detection** protects first-party agent names from being shadowed by custom packages. The `AGENT_TO_PACKAGE` dictionary maps every known first-party agent name to its owning package (e.g., `"transcriptomics_expert"` → `"lobster-transcriptomics"`). When a custom package registers an agent with a reserved name, `_check_agent_name_collisions()` raises `ComponentConflictError`. This prevents a malicious or poorly-designed plugin from hijacking the supervisor's routing table.

The `diagnose_missing_agent()` function provides a third safety layer: when a user references an agent that doesn't exist, it distinguishes between three cases — (1) known agent in an uninstalled package (produces install command), (2) installed agent with broken dependencies (shows the load error), and (3) truly unknown agent (suggests `lobster agents list`). This diagnostic logic uses `AGENT_TO_PACKAGE` and `_failed_entries` to produce actionable messages rather than opaque errors.

Sources: [component_registry.py](lobster/core/component_registry.py#L132-L266), [component_registry.py](lobster/core/component_registry.py#L389-L438), [component_registry.py](lobster/core/component_registry.py#L550-L559)

## Entry Points in Practice: The Transcriptomics Package

The `lobster-transcriptomics` package serves as the reference implementation for the agent plugin pattern. Its `pyproject.toml` declares two entry point groups:

```toml
[project.entry-points."lobster.agents"]
transcriptomics_expert = "lobster.agents.transcriptomics.transcriptomics_expert:AGENT_CONFIG"
annotation_expert = "lobster.agents.transcriptomics.annotation_expert:AGENT_CONFIG"
de_analysis_expert = "lobster.agents.transcriptomics.de_analysis_expert:AGENT_CONFIG"

[project.entry-points."lobster.states"]
TranscriptomicsExpertState = "lobster.agents.transcriptomics.state:TranscriptomicsExpertState"
```

Three key patterns are visible here: (1) multiple agents per package, each with its own `AGENT_CONFIG` in a separate module; (2) entry point names matching agent names exactly, which the core `pyproject.toml` documents as a requirement for `queue_preparers` and `download_services` groups; and (3) the `lobster.states` group for state schema discovery, allowing the supervisor to inspect state types without importing agent code. The package depends on `lobster-ai~=1.1.0` as its core constraint, which the compatibility checker validates at load time.

The core `pyproject.toml` mirrors this pattern for service and data-access entry points, registering five database-specific download services and queue preparers:

| Entry Point Name | Download Service | Queue Preparer |
|---|---|---|
| `geo` | `GEODownloadService` | `GEOQueuePreparer` |
| `sra` | `SRADownloadService` | `SRAQueuePreparer` |
| `pride` | `PRIDEDownloadService` | `PRIDEQueuePreparer` |
| `massive` | `MassIVEDownloadService` | `MassIVEQueuePreparer` |
| `metabolights` | `MetaboLightsDownloadService` | `MetaboLightsQueuePreparer` |

Sources: [pyproject.toml (transcriptomics)](packages/lobster-transcriptomics/pyproject.toml#L66-L74), [pyproject.toml (core)](pyproject.toml#L266-L301)

## Navigation

- **Previous**: [Agent Registry and Discovery](7-agent-registry-and-discovery) — how discovered agents populate the supervisor's routing table
- **Next**: [AQUADIF Tool Taxonomy](9-aquadif-tool-taxonomy) — the metadata framework that plugin tools must implement
- **Related**: [Scaffold and Package Validation](10-scaffold-and-package-validation) — deeper dive into validation rules and template structure

# AQUADIF Tool Taxonomy



Lobster classifies every tool in its multi-agent graph under the **AQUADIF** taxonomy — a six-category scheme whose acronym encodes the full lifecycle of a bioinformatics workflow: **A**nalyze, **QU**ery, **A** (Import/Access), **D**elegate, **I** (Code Execution / Iterate), and **F**ramework (Utility). Each tool declares its AQUADIF category (or categories) via a `.metadata` dictionary attached at factory-creation time, and the runtime `AquadifMonitor` consumes this metadata to produce real-time session telemetry — category distribution, provenance compliance, and code-execution audit trails — without ever interfering with tool execution. This page explains the taxonomy's design rationale, the metadata contract every tool must satisfy, the monitor's fail-open architecture, and the patterns you follow when adding new tools or entire agent packages.

Sources: [aquadif_monitor.py](lobster/core/governance/aquadif_monitor.py#L1-L50), [graph.py](lobster/agents/graph.py#L1-L50)

## AQUADIF Category Definitions

The six categories are not merely labels — they encode behavioral contracts that the monitoring layer, the provenance system, and the supervisor's routing logic all depend on. A tool may belong to multiple categories (e.g., a knowledgebase tool that both queries an external API and returns structured data for downstream analysis), and the monitor increments counters for every category listed in the tool's metadata. The table below defines each category, its provenance expectation, and representative tools from the codebase.

| Category | Full Name | Provenance Required | Representative Tools | Primary Agent(s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ANALYZE** | Data Analysis | Yes | `execute_custom_code` (with `persist=True`) | data_expert, transcriptomics_expert |
| **QUERY** | External Data Query | Yes | `search_pubmed`, `search_geo`, `search_pride` | research_agent, metadata_assistant |
| **IMPORT** | Data Import / Access | Yes | Download orchestrator tools, `map_cross_database_ids` | data_expert, genomics_expert |
| **DELEGATE** | Agent Delegation | No | `handoff_to_research_agent`, `handoff_to_transcriptomics_expert` | supervisor |
| **CODE_EXEC** | Custom Code Execution | Yes | `execute_custom_code` (always carries CODE_EXEC) | data_expert, metadata_assistant |
| **UTILITY** | Framework / Utility | No | `list_files`, `read_file`, `retrieve_agent_result`, `get_content_from_workspace` | all agents |

> [!TIP]
> Tools in the **ANALYZE**, **QUERY**, **IMPORT**, and **CODE_EXEC** categories set `"provenance": True` in their metadata, which causes the `AquadifMonitor` to pre-set their provenance status to `"missing"` on first invocation. The status only transitions to `"real_ir"` or `"hollow_ir"` when `DataManagerV2.log_tool_usage()` is called — tools that skip this call surface as compliance gaps in the session summary.

The provenance column is not advisory — it is enforced observationally. When `record_tool_invocation` fires, the monitor checks `metadata["provenance"]`; if `True`, the tool name is seeded into `_provenance_status` with value `"missing"`. Only a subsequent call to `record_provenance_call` (triggered from `DataManagerV2.log_tool_usage`) can promote the status to `"real_ir"` or `"hollow_ir"`. Tools that never call `log_tool_usage` remain stuck at `"missing"`, surfacing as compliance gaps in `get_session_summary()`.

Sources: [aquadif_monitor.py](lobster/core/governance/aquadif_monitor.py#L82-L162), [store_tools.py](lobster/tools/store_tools.py#L95-L113), [filesystem_tools.py](lobster/tools/filesystem_tools.py#L1-L50)

## The Metadata Contract

Every LangChain `@tool` function in Lobster must carry a `.metadata` dictionary and a `.tags` list once it is wired into the agent graph. The metadata dict has two keys — `"categories"` (a list of AQUADIF category strings) and `"provenance"` (a boolean) — and the tags list mirrors the categories for downstream filtering. This contract is established at factory-creation time, not at invocation time, which means the metadata is static and inspectable before any tool runs.

```python
# Example: delegation tool metadata (DELEGATE category, no provenance)
invoke_agent.metadata = {"categories": ["DELEGATE"], "provenance": False}
invoke_agent.tags = ["DELEGATE"]

# Example: utility tool metadata (UTILITY category, no provenance)
retrieve_agent_result.metadata = {"categories": ["UTILITY"], "provenance": False}
retrieve_agent_result.tags = ["UTILITY"]
```

The factory pattern is the enforcement mechanism. All shared tools — `create_execute_custom_code_tool`, `create_filesystem_tools`, `create_retrieve_agent_result_tool`, and the delegation tool factories in `graph.py` — attach metadata inside the factory closure before returning the tool. This ensures that no tool can accidentally enter the graph without AQUADIF classification, because the factory is the only sanctioned creation path.

Sources: [graph.py](lobster/agents/graph.py#L200-L230), [store_tools.py](lobster/tools/store_tools.py#L95-L113), [custom_code_tool.py](lobster/tools/custom_code_tool.py#L1-L50)

## AquadifMonitor Architecture

The `AquadifMonitor` is a runtime introspection service instantiated once per session inside `AgentClient.__init__`. It has **zero imports from `lobster.*`** — a deliberate design choice to prevent circular imports, since the callback module that calls `record_tool_invocation` already imports the monitor. All public methods are **fail-open**: exceptions are caught internally and silently swallowed, ensuring the monitor can never crash a tool invocation.

The monitor collects three orthogonal data streams through two injection points:

1. **`record_tool_invocation(tool_name, current_agent)`** — called exclusively from `TokenTrackingCallback.on_tool_start`. This is the single injection point for invocation counting; other callback handlers (`TerminalCallbackHandler`, `StreamingCallbackHandler`) must not call it to avoid double-counting in cloud sessions.
2. **`record_provenance_call(tool_name, has_real_ir)`** — called from `DataManagerV2.log_tool_usage`. This observes the actual provenance recording at the authoritative site, using direct boolean observation rather than brittle output-string parsing.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Injection Points
        A["TokenTrackingCallback<br/>.on_tool_start()"]
        B["DataManagerV2<br/>.log_tool_usage()"]
    end

    subgraph AquadifMonitor
        C["record_tool_invocation()"]
        D["record_provenance_call()"]
        E[("_category_counts<br/>{ANALYZE: 3, QUERY: 1, ...}")]
        F[("_tool_invocation_counts<br/>{tool_name: count}")]
        G[("_provenance_status<br/>{tool_name: real_ir|hollow_ir|missing}")]
        H[("_code_exec_log<br/>deque(maxlen=100)")]
    end

    subgraph Consumers
        I["get_session_summary()<br/>→ Cloud SSE enrichment"]
        J["get_category_distribution()<br/>→ Dashboard telemetry"]
        K["get_provenance_status()<br/>→ Compliance audit"]
    end

    A --> C
    B --> D
    C --> E
    C --> F
    C --> H
    C --> G
    D --> G
    E --> I
    F --> I
    G --> I
    H --> I
    E --> J
    G --> K
```

Thread safety follows a split strategy: simple dictionary counter increments (single CPython bytecode operations protected by the GIL) run without locks, while compound mutations — deque append plus dict update, or provenance status transitions — acquire `self._lock`. Lock-held sections are kept short, and no method calls another method while holding the lock, preventing reentrancy bugs.

Sources: [aquadif_monitor.py](lobster/core/governance/aquadif_monitor.py#L52-L162), [aquadif_monitor.py](lobster/core/governance/aquadif_monitor.py#L200-L269), [aquadif_monitor.py](lobster/core/aquadif_monitor.py#L1-L12)

## Provenance Status State Machine

The provenance status for each tool follows a strict upgrade-only state machine. A tool starts at `"missing"` (seeded on first invocation if `provenance: True`), can transition to `"hollow_ir"` when `log_tool_usage` is called with `ir=None` (the bridge pattern for tools that are tracked but don't produce an `AnalysisStep` notebook), and can upgrade to `"real_ir"` when a full `AnalysisStep` is recorded. Crucially, `"real_ir"` cannot be downgraded — if a tool achieves full provenance compliance, subsequent `ir=None` calls are no-ops.

| Transition | Trigger | Semantics |
|---|---|---|
| (none) → `missing` | `record_tool_invocation` with `provenance: True` | Tool invoked, provenance expected but not yet recorded |
| `missing` → `hollow_ir` | `record_provenance_call(has_real_ir=False)` | `log_tool_usage` called with `ir=None` (bridge pattern) |
| `missing` → `real_ir` | `record_provenance_call(has_real_ir=True)` | Full `AnalysisStep` IR recorded |
| `hollow_ir` → `real_ir` | `record_provenance_call(has_real_ir=True)` | Upgraded from bridge to full provenance |
| `real_ir` → `real_ir` | `record_provenance_call(has_real_ir=True)` | No-op; cannot downgrade |

This state machine is implemented in `record_provenance_call` with an explicit guard: `if self._provenance_status.get(tool_name) != "real_ir"`, ensuring that once a tool achieves full compliance, it remains compliant regardless of subsequent invocations that might use the bridge pattern.

Sources: [aquadif_monitor.py](lobster/core/governance/aquadif_monitor.py#L142-L180)

## Tool Metadata Map Construction

The `AquadifMonitor` requires a `tool_metadata_map` at construction time — a dictionary mapping tool names to their AQUADIF metadata. However, the monitor is instantiated before the LangGraph agent graph is built, creating a temporal dependency: tools don't exist yet when the monitor is created. The codebase resolves this with a two-phase initialization pattern.

In phase one, the monitor is constructed with an empty map: `AquadifMonitor(tool_metadata_map={})`. In phase two, after `graph.py` creates all tools via their factories, it iterates the tool list and builds the metadata map from each tool's `.metadata` attribute, then assigns it to `monitor._tool_metadata_map`. This deferred assignment is safe because no tool invocations can occur before the graph is fully constructed.

```python
# Phase 1: monitor created with empty map (in AgentClient.__init__)
self.aquadif_monitor = AquadifMonitor(tool_metadata_map={})

# Phase 2: map populated after graph construction (in graph.py)
tool_metadata_map = {}
for t in all_tools:
    if hasattr(t, 'metadata') and t.metadata:
        tool_metadata_map[t.name] = t.metadata
self.aquadif_monitor._tool_metadata_map = tool_metadata_map
```

> [!TIP]
> When adding a new tool, you do not need to touch the monitor code. As long as your tool's factory attaches `.metadata = {"categories": [...], "provenance": bool}`, the graph construction phase will automatically include it in the metadata map. The only integration point is ensuring your tool calls `data_manager.log_tool_usage()` if `provenance: True`.

Sources: [aquadif_monitor.py](lobster/core/governance/aquadif_monitor.py#L75-L100), [graph.py](lobster/agents/graph.py#L399-L500)

## Category Distribution Across Tool Submodules

The following table maps each tool submodule to its primary AQUADIF categories, showing how the taxonomy spans the full tool surface. Tools in `lobster/tools/providers/` are uniformly QUERY-category (they wrap external database APIs), while tools in `lobster/tools/` proper span UTILITY, CODE_EXEC, and IMPORT depending on their function.

| Submodule | Tool(s) | AQUADIF Categories | Provenance |
|---|---|---|---|
| `custom_code_tool` | `execute_custom_code` | CODE_EXEC, ANALYZE | Yes |
| `workspace_tool` | `get_content_from_workspace`, `list_available_modalities`, `delete_from_workspace` | UTILITY | No |
| `filesystem_tools` | `list_files`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `glob_files`, `grep_files`, `shell_execute` | UTILITY | No |
| `store_tools` | `retrieve_agent_result` | UTILITY | No |
| `knowledgebase_tools` | `map_cross_database_ids`, `variant_consequence`, `sequence_retrieval` | QUERY, IMPORT | Yes |
| `download_orchestrator` | (orchestration layer, not a `@tool`) | — | — |
| `providers/pubmed_provider` | `search_pubmed` | QUERY | Yes |
| `providers/geo_provider` | `search_geo` | QUERY | Yes |
| `providers/pdb_provider` | `search_pdb` | QUERY | Yes |
| `providers/pride_provider` | `search_pride` | QUERY | Yes |
| `graph.py` (delegation) | `handoff_to_*` | DELEGATE | No |

Note that `download_orchestrator.py` is not itself a `@tool` — it is a service class that routes to `IDownloadService` implementations registered via `lobster.download_services` entry points. The actual download tools that wrap it carry the IMPORT category.

Sources: [custom_code_tool.py](lobster/tools/custom_code_tool.py#L1-L50), [workspace_tool.py](lobster/tools/workspace_tool.py#L1-L50), [filesystem_tools.py](lobster/tools/filesystem_tools.py#L1-L50), [store_tools.py](lobster/tools/store_tools.py#L1-L50), [knowledgebase_tools.py](lobster/tools/knowledgebase_tools.py#L1-L50), [download_orchestrator.py](lobster/tools/download_orchestrator.py#L1-L50)

## Adding a New Tool to the Taxonomy

When you add a new tool — whether in `lobster/tools/` or inside a domain package — you must satisfy three requirements to integrate with AQUADIF:

1. **Attach metadata in the factory function.** Every tool created via the factory pattern must set `.metadata` and `.tags` before the factory returns. Choose categories that reflect the tool's primary behavioral contract (a tool that fetches data from an external API is QUERY; one that runs user-supplied Python is CODE_EXEC). Set `provenance: True` only if the tool produces an `AnalysisStep` IR or calls `data_manager.log_tool_usage()`.

2. **Call `log_tool_usage` if provenance is required.** Tools with `provenance: True` must call `data_manager.log_tool_usage(tool_name=..., parameters=..., description=..., ir=...)` at the end of their execution. If the tool produces a full `AnalysisStep`, pass it as `ir`; if not, pass `ir=None` (the bridge pattern, which the monitor records as `"hollow_ir"`). Omitting this call leaves the tool stuck at `"missing"` in the provenance status.

3. **Register via entry points for discovery.** If the tool lives in a domain package, ensure the package's `pyproject.toml` declares the appropriate entry point group (`lobster.agents`, `lobster.providers`, `lobster.adapters`) so the `ComponentRegistry` can discover it. The graph construction phase automatically includes discovered tools in the monitor's metadata map.

```python
# Minimal pattern for a new QUERY tool with provenance
def create_my_query_tool(data_manager: DataManagerV2):
    @tool
    async def search_database(query: str) -> str:
        """Search external database for bioinformatics records."""
        result = await _do_search(query)
        data_manager.log_tool_usage(
            tool_name="search_database",
            parameters={"query": query},
            description=f"Searched for '{query}'",
            ir=None,  # Bridge pattern — no AnalysisStep
        )
        return result

    search_database.metadata = {"categories": ["QUERY"], "provenance": True}
    search_database.tags = ["QUERY"]
    return search_database
```

Sources: [custom_code_tool.py](lobster/tools/custom_code_tool.py#L140-L200), [store_tools.py](lobster/tools/store_tools.py#L88-L113), [component_registry.py](lobster/core/component_registry.py#L1-L60)

## Session Summary and Cloud Integration

The `get_session_summary()` method produces a structured snapshot of the monitor's state, designed for Omics-OS Cloud SSE (Server-Sent Events) enrichment. It acquires the lock once, builds a consistent view of all four internal data structures, and returns a dictionary with five keys:

| Key | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `category_distribution` | `Dict[str, int]` | Per-category invocation counts |
| `provenance_status` | `Dict[str, List[str]]` | Tools grouped by `real_ir`, `hollow_ir`, `missing` |
| `code_exec_count` | `int` | Total CODE_EXEC invocations in the bounded log |
| `code_exec_log` | `List[Dict]` | Last 100 CODE_EXEC entries (tool_name, timestamp, agent) |
| `total_invocations` | `int` | Sum of all tool invocation counts |

This summary mirrors the pattern established by `TokenTrackingCallback.get_usage_summary()` and is consumed by the cloud layer to provide real-time session dashboards — showing which AQUADIF categories are active, whether provenance is compliant, and which agents are executing custom code. The bounded deque (`maxlen=100`) ensures memory safety in long-running sessions, auto-evicting the oldest entries when capacity is reached.

Sources: [aquadif_monitor.py](lobster/core/governance/aquadif_monitor.py#L219-L269)

## Backward Compatibility Shim

The monitor was originally defined at `lobster.core.aquadif_monitor` but has been migrated to `lobster.core.governance.aquadif_monitor` to co-locate it with other governance modules (`license_manager`). The old path now contains a thin shim that emits a `DeprecationWarning` and re-exports all names via `from lobster.core.governance.aquadif_monitor import *`. This shim will be removed in v2.0.0. All new code should import from the governance submodule directly.

Sources: [aquadif_monitor.py](lobster/core/aquadif_monitor.py#L1-L12)
